slides: So, before you practice, let's go over the whole topic. About three minutes.
Every tool, every trap. Short, and quick.
Now, before you do any arithmetic... translate first.
A big power? Break the base into primes. Once the bases are equal, things start cancelling.
A root inside a root? Turn it into a fractional exponent.
And don't compute giant numbers just because you can.
Some questions hide a pattern you already know.
You know x plus y, and x times y? Then build x squared plus y squared directly. You don't need to find x and y.
a to the power of b equals b to the power of a... that only happens with two and four. And only for whole numbers.
Equal powers added together? Just count the copies.
Okay, a root inside a root: you multiply the indices.
Two times two... so it's a fourth root.
And if there's a factor in front of the inner root? Bring it inside first. Squared.
Now, say x has a strange power, and you want x alone.
Raise both sides to the reciprocal power. Minus a half, times minus two, is one.
Then check it. One twenty-fifth to the power of minus a half is twenty-five to the power of a half. That's five. So it works.
This one is the difference of squares, but with roots.
a minus b, over root a minus root b? Split the top, and cancel.
And a difference of roots at the bottom? Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate.
Now, an equation that's already a product equal to zero.
Each factor can be zero. So root x is zero, or root x is five.
And never divide by root x. If you do, you lose x equals zero.
A close relative: root x equals x. Square it, and x equals x squared. So x times, x minus one, is zero.
So only zero and one. And it's the same for x squared equals x.
So when is a power equal to one?
Base one. Base minus one, with an even exponent. Or exponent zero... with a base that isn't zero.
Now, an "or" claim is necessarily true if every allowed case makes one part true. To kill it, you just need one case where both parts are false.
Now, some choices come as: IF something, THEN something.
Treat the IF as one more given. And cross out the cases it rules out.
Then check the THEN in every case that's left. One case where it fails... and the choice is out.
Say a to the power of b equals one, and a and b are whole numbers. If a is negative, two cases are left. Base minus one with an even exponent... or exponent zero.
And zero is even too. So it's true.
Well, an IF that rules out no case proves nothing. Then the THEN has to hold in every case anyway.
Every question has two routes.
The laws, step by step. Or plug in numbers... or try the choices.
But before you trust one number, check that the choices give different values. If two of them tie, try another number.
And pick a number whose roots come out clean. Like eighty-one.
Can't split a root nicely? Estimate it. Root fifty is a little over seven. Then compare with the choices.

And watch the traps. Root a plus root b is not the root of a plus b. Two and four, only for whole numbers. And never divide by root x.
